title: No Other Name: The First Arrest
summary: The temple leaders arrest Peter and John for proclaiming the resurrection in Jesus. Before the council, Peter, filled with the Spirit, declares that the lame man was healed by the name of the crucified and risen Jesus, the only name by which people must be saved. Warned not to speak in that name, the apostles refuse; the believers pray for boldness, the place is shaken, and the community shares its goods so that no one is in need, with Barnabas as an example.
story: The healing in chapter 3 drew a crowd, and Peter's sermon in Solomon's Colonnade has not finished when the authorities arrive. This is the first open conflict between the church and the Jerusalem leadership, the same leaders who handed Jesus over to Pilate. The pattern Jesus warned of (Luke 21:12-15) begins: his followers are brought before rulers and given words to speak. The chapter moves from arrest to trial to release, then to the church's prayer and the Spirit's answer, and closes with a portrait of the community's generosity that prepares for the story of Ananias and Sapphira in chapter 5.
historical:
The arresting party includes the captain of the temple, a senior priestly officer responsible for order in the temple and commander of its Levite police, and the Sadducees. The Sadducees were a party drawn largely from the priestly aristocracy and wealthy families. They rejected the Pharisees' traditions of interpretation, held closely to the written law (some early Christian writers say they accepted only the five books of Moses, though that is uncertain), cooperated with Roman rule, and denied the resurrection of the dead (Luke 20:27; Acts 23:8). Preaching that the resurrection had already begun in Jesus was doubly offensive to them.

The council, called the Sanhedrin, was the highest Jewish court in Jerusalem, composed of chief priests, elders (leading laymen), and scribes (experts in the law), presided over by the high priest. Caiaphas was the ruling high priest; Luke calls Annas high priest because the former holder of the office kept the title and much of the influence. John and Alexander are otherwise unknown, though some manuscripts read Jonathan, and a son of Annas named Jonathan did later serve as high priest. The prayer of verses 24 to 30 names Herod (Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, before whom Jesus appeared in Luke 23:6-12) and Pontius Pilate as the kings and rulers of Psalm 2.
cultural:
Unschooled and ordinary (verse 13) does not mean Peter and John could not read. The first word describes men without formal training in the law under a recognized teacher, and the second describes a layman, a private person without professional standing. The council is struck that such men can argue from Scripture with confidence, and they recognize the mark of Jesus, who was also untrained by their standards (John 7:15).

The community's sharing of goods was voluntary, as Peter's words in 5:4 make clear; it was not the abolition of private property but the willingness to treat one's property as available to others in need. Laying gifts at the apostles' feet was a gesture of placing them under their authority for distribution. Deuteronomy 15:4 had promised that there would be no poor among God's people if they obeyed him, and Luke's note that there were no needy ones among them may echo that promise. Barnabas is a Levite, a member of the tribe traditionally set apart for temple service, from Cyprus; he will become a key figure in Acts, vouching for Saul and later traveling with him.
literary: The chapter alternates public and private scenes: arrest (1-4), trial (5-12), deliberation behind closed doors (13-17), verdict and response (18-22), prayer among believers (23-31), and summary of the community's life (32-37). Peter's defense is brief and pointed. He turns an inquiry about a kind service to a lame man into a proclamation about the builders who rejected the cornerstone (Psalm 118:22). The believers' prayer is the longest prayer in Acts and is shaped by Scripture: it opens by praising the Creator, quotes Psalm 2, applies it to the events of Jesus' death, and asks not for safety but for boldness. The word boldness frames the section (4:13, 29, 31).

outline.t: Arrest by the priests and Sadducees; the church grows
Before the council: salvation in no other name
The council confers: we cannot deny it
Forbidden to speak; the apostles refuse
The church prays for boldness and is filled with the Spirit
One heart and soul: sharing possessions; Barnabas

doctrines.note: Peter declares that salvation exists in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven by which people must be saved. The church has always read this as a claim that Jesus is the unique Savior. The name of Jesus heals the lame man, and the same name saves.

The believers pray to the Sovereign Lord, the Creator, and confess that the conspiracy against Jesus carried out what God's hand and will had decided beforehand. They do not pray for their enemies to be removed but for boldness, trusting that the same God rules over their present threats.

Peter is filled with the Holy Spirit before he speaks to the council (4:8), and the whole community is filled again after prayer (4:31). In Acts filling with the Spirit can happen more than once and is often linked with bold speech.
The church is of one heart and soul, and its unity shows up in how it handles money. Generosity is not a program but the overflow of grace, and it serves the apostles' testimony to the resurrection.

words.note: Parresia, boldness, frankness, or freedom of speech. In the Greek world it described the right of a free citizen to speak openly in the assembly. In Acts it becomes a mark of the Spirit's work: ordinary men speak openly before the powerful. The believers pray for it (4:29) and receive it (4:31).

Soteria, salvation, deliverance, or rescue, including healing and safety. The lame man was saved, made whole, in the name of Jesus (4:9 uses the related verb), and Peter moves at once to the salvation that all people need. The word covers both bodily and spiritual rescue, and Peter's point is that both come from the same Lord.

Paraklesis, encouragement, comfort, or exhortation. Barnabas's nickname, Son of Encouragement, uses this word; a son of something in Hebrew idiom is someone marked by it. The word is related to parakletos, the title Jesus gives the Holy Spirit in John 14 to 16, one who comes alongside.

christ: Peter's defense makes the chapter's claim about Christ plain: Jesus of Nazareth, crucified by the leaders and raised by God, is the stone the builders rejected who has become the cornerstone, the foundation stone that holds the building together. Jesus himself had applied Psalm 118 to himself (Luke 20:17). The believers' prayer calls him God's holy servant and Anointed One, the king of Psalm 2 against whom the nations rage in vain. And the apostles' boldness is traced to having been with Jesus. The name of Jesus, meaning his person and authority, heals, saves, and is the one thing the council cannot stop the apostles from speaking.

hard.q: Is it arrogant or unfair to claim that salvation comes through Jesus alone?
hard.a:
Acts 4:12 is one of the New Testament's clearest statements that Jesus is the only Savior, and it is offensive to many modern readers who see all religions as paths to the same end. Christians have responded in several ways. Many hold that the verse means what it says for everyone: salvation comes only through Christ, and only to those who hear and believe (often called exclusivism). Others, sometimes called inclusivists, agree that all salvation comes through Christ alone but believe that God may save some who never heard of him, through Christ's work applied in ways known only to God. Religious pluralism, the view that many religions save equally, has been rejected by the historic church as incompatible with this verse and with the confession that Jesus is Lord.

It helps to see the claim in its setting. Peter is not a powerful man imposing his religion on the weak; he is a prisoner on trial before the powerful. He is not claiming that Christians are better than others but that God has acted in one person for everyone. The claim is exclusive in its object but open in its invitation, since the name is given to men, all people, under heaven. Christians differ on the fate of those who never hear, which the Bible does not address directly, but they agree that the claim concerns Jesus, not themselves.

questions: The council noticed that Peter and John had been with Jesus. What would people notice about you that could only be explained by time spent with him?
When threatened, the church prayed for boldness rather than safety. What would change if you prayed that way about the pressures you face?
The believers treated their possessions as available to anyone in need. What would that look like in practice for you or your church?
